claims.text: Applying an adaptive nanolaminate surface treatment to CoCrFeNi will produce an in situ lubricious oxide glaze during sliding at temperatures of at least 600 °C.
The nanolaminate treatment will retain a hard, low-friction surface at room temperature.
The treatment will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate relative to untreated CoCrFeNi throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
The nanolaminate will transform gradually under sliding-induced heating.
At ambient temperature, the layered coating will provide a hard, wear-resistant interface.
At elevated temperatures, reaction of the upper laminate layers with environmental oxygen will form a robust, lubricious oxide glaze.
The multilayer architecture will preserve a mechanically stable, dense near-surface layer at lower temperatures.
The multilayer architecture will facilitate formation of a continuous and adherent oxide layer at higher temperatures.
Sliding stresses cause localized frictional heating at the treated surface.
At room temperature, the nanolaminate simultaneously maintains high hardness and low shear strength.
High-temperature sliding at or above about 600 °C involves surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation.
High-temperature sliding softens metallic surfaces and increases their susceptibility to chemical instability and severe wear.
A tribo-oxidation-derived oxide glaze can provide solid lubrication and produce a gentler wear regime.
The proposed oxide glaze will reduce adhesion and interfacial shear.
The adaptive transition will switch the dominant wear mechanism from plastic deformation or adhesive wear to oxidative lubrication.
The treated material will maintain low friction and reduced wear at high temperature despite thermal softening of the base alloy.
Untreated CoCrFeNi has increased friction and wear variability at elevated temperature because of unstable oxide formation and microstructural softening.
The treatment will remain effective under both low and high normal loads in oxidizing ambient air.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the laminate and CoCrFeNi substrate may reduce durability during repeated thermal cycling.
